section_content.title: Culture & Stakeholders

body.text: **Corporate culture** is the unwritten code that governs 'how things are done around here'. It shapes employee behaviour, management style, and the firm's ability to adapt. Culture is not what the mission statement says — it is what people actually do when nobody is watching.

**Handy's cultural typology** identifies four types. **Power culture** — decisions radiate from a central figure (common in start-ups and family firms). **Role culture** — authority flows from job titles and formal rules (typical of large bureaucracies). **Task culture** — teams form around projects, with expertise trumping hierarchy. **Person culture** — the organisation exists to serve the individuals within it (law chambers, medical practices).

A **strong culture** means values are widely shared and deeply held — this improves consistency and motivation but can become a barrier to change because 'the way we've always done it' resists new ideas. A **weak culture** has no dominant set of values, making the firm adaptable but directionless.

steps: Strong culture established
Employees align around shared values
Consistency and identity strengthen
But resistance to new ways of working grows
body.result: Culture becomes both an asset and a barrier to change

sections.title: Corporate Culture
sections.keyIdea: Corporate culture is the shared values, beliefs, and norms that shape how people behave inside a business — it is invisible but determines everything from decision speed to willingness to change.
sections.examMatters: Examiners want you to classify culture using Handy's typology and then evaluate its impact. Always link to context: a power culture suits a start-up needing fast decisions, but becomes a bottleneck when the firm grows and the founder cannot oversee everything.

realExample.text: Google deliberately cultivates a task culture — cross-functional project teams, flat structures, and '20% time' for personal projects. This drives innovation but can create coordination challenges as the company scales beyond 180,000 employees.

sections.misconception: Students describe culture as something managers can simply choose or switch overnight. Wrong — culture is deeply embedded in daily habits and takes years to shift. Instead write: culture evolves from repeated behaviours and shared experiences; changing it requires sustained leadership effort, not just a new mission statement.

body.text: A **stakeholder** is any individual or group with an interest in the business — employees, customers, suppliers, shareholders, local communities, government, and pressure groups. Their interests often conflict: shareholders want maximum dividends while employees want higher wages.

**Mendelow's power-interest matrix** classifies stakeholders into four quadrants. **High power, high interest** — key players who must be managed closely (e.g. major shareholders, regulators). **High power, low interest** — keep satisfied (e.g. government). **Low power, high interest** — keep informed (e.g. local community). **Low power, low interest** — minimal effort needed.

The **shareholder vs stakeholder debate** is central. **Friedman** argued the only social responsibility of business is to increase profits for shareholders — anything else is misusing other people's money. **Freeman** countered that businesses depend on all stakeholders and must balance their interests to survive long-term.

steps: Identify all stakeholders
Map power and interest for each
Classify using Mendelow's matrix
body.result: Strategy tailored to each group — key players managed closely, others monitored

sections.title: Stakeholder Analysis
sections.keyIdea: Stakeholders are any group affected by or able to affect a business — Mendelow's matrix maps them by power and interest, revealing who the firm must prioritise and who it can safely monitor.
sections.examMatters: A strong exam answer uses Mendelow's matrix to structure analysis. Draw the 2x2 grid, place specific stakeholders in quadrants with justification, and explain the management strategy for each. Examiners reward application to the case study, not generic descriptions.

realExample.text: The Volkswagen emissions scandal (2015) is a textbook stakeholder failure. VW prioritised shareholder returns above all else, cheating emissions tests to boost sales. When exposed, it destroyed trust with customers, regulators, and employees — costing over €30 billion in fines and wiping out years of shareholder value.

sections.misconception: Students treat Mendelow's matrix as static. Wrong — stakeholders move between quadrants as circumstances change. A quiet community group (low power) can become high power overnight through media attention. Instead write: stakeholder mapping is dynamic; firms must constantly reassess where groups sit as events unfold.

takeaway: Handy's four culture types: power, role, task, person — each suits different business contexts.
Strong culture drives consistency but resists change; weak culture is adaptable but lacks direction.
Mendelow's matrix (power vs interest) determines stakeholder management strategy — it is dynamic, not fixed.

section_content.title: Ethics & CSR

body.text: **Business ethics** are the moral principles that guide how a firm behaves. A business can be entirely legal yet deeply unethical — paying minimum wage while executives earn millions, or selling products known to cause harm but not yet regulated.

Ethical behaviour covers treatment of workers (fair wages, safe conditions), honesty with customers (transparent pricing, truthful advertising), environmental responsibility (beyond legal minimums), and supply chain standards (refusing to use exploitative suppliers).

The business case **for** ethics: builds brand loyalty, attracts talent, reduces regulatory risk, and avoids costly scandals. The case **against**: higher short-term costs, competitive disadvantage if rivals cut corners, and difficulty measuring ethical impact on the bottom line.

steps: Firm adopts ethical stance beyond legal requirements
Higher costs in short run
Reputation and trust build over time
body.result: Long-run competitive advantage through brand loyalty and reduced risk

sections.title: Business Ethics
sections.keyIdea: Ethics goes beyond legal compliance — it asks what a business should do, not just what it is allowed to do, and the gap between the two is where reputational risk lives.
sections.examMatters: Examiners test evaluation — can you argue both sides? A strong answer acknowledges that ethics can raise costs and reduce competitiveness in the short run, but argues that long-run reputational benefits and risk reduction often outweigh those costs. Always use real examples.

realExample.text: Patagonia builds ethics into its core business model — it famously ran an advert saying 'Don't Buy This Jacket' to discourage overconsumption. This radical honesty has built fierce customer loyalty and allowed premium pricing, proving ethics and profit can align.

sections.misconception: Students assume ethical behaviour always costs money with no return. Wrong — unethical behaviour often costs far more in the long run through fines, lawsuits, and lost customers. Instead write: ethics has a cost, but the cost of unethical behaviour (reputational damage, regulatory fines, loss of trust) is typically higher.

body.text: **Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)** refers to a business voluntarily going beyond legal requirements to consider the social, environmental, and ethical impacts of its operations. It covers environmental sustainability, community engagement, fair labour practices, and charitable giving.

**Arguments for CSR**: enhanced brand reputation and customer loyalty, ability to attract and retain talented employees, reduced risk of regulatory intervention, long-term shareholder value through sustainable practices, and differentiation from competitors.

**Arguments against CSR**: Friedman's view that profit is the only social responsibility (CSR diverts resources from shareholders), the risk of **greenwashing** (superficial CSR used as marketing), difficulty measuring genuine social impact, and potential competitive disadvantage against firms that ignore CSR.

steps: Firm adopts CSR programme
Stakeholders respond positively
Brand value and loyalty increase
body.result: But only if CSR is genuine — greenwashing destroys trust faster than no CSR at all

sections.title: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
sections.keyIdea: CSR is a firm's voluntary commitment to act in the interests of society beyond its legal obligations — but the line between genuine CSR and greenwashing is where the real exam debate lives.
sections.examMatters: The highest-mark answers evaluate CSR critically. Don't just list benefits — challenge whether CSR is genuine or greenwashing, whether it actually changes business behaviour or just marketing, and whether Friedman's profit-only argument has merit in a world of climate change and social media accountability.

realExample.text: BP rebranded itself as 'Beyond Petroleum' with a green sunflower logo in 2000, spending millions on CSR marketing. Then the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster killed 11 workers and caused the worst oil spill in US history — revealing the CSR as greenwashing. BP's brand damage lasted over a decade.

sections.misconception: Students treat CSR and ethics as the same thing. Wrong — ethics is about moral principles guiding daily decisions; CSR is a broader strategic commitment to society. A firm can behave ethically (not lying to customers) without having a formal CSR programme. Instead write: ethics guides individual decisions; CSR is a deliberate organisational strategy to benefit wider society.

takeaway: Ethics is about what a firm should do beyond legal compliance — the gap is where reputational risk sits.
CSR is a voluntary strategic commitment; greenwashing is CSR as marketing without substance.
Friedman vs Freeman: profit-only vs stakeholder balance — examiners want you to argue both sides with examples.

steps: Values and norms shape employee behaviour
Strong culture → consistency and motivation
But resistance to change if culture becomes rigid
flow.result: Culture is a strategic asset when aligned with objectives, a liability when outdated

section_notes.title: Corporate Culture

items.text: Corporate culture — the set of shared values, attitudes, and practices that characterise an organisation and influence how people behave within it.
Strong culture — one where values are widely shared and deeply held, giving employees a clear sense of identity and purpose.
Handy's culture types — Power (central control), Role (bureaucratic), Task (project-based), Person (individual-focused); each suits different organisations.
A strong culture can be a competitive advantage — employees are motivated, consistent, and aligned with the brand (e.g. Apple's innovation culture).
But a strong culture can also be a barrier to change — 'the way we do things here' may prevent the firm from adapting to new market conditions.
During mergers, culture clash is the most common reason for failure — two strong but incompatible cultures create conflict, lower morale, and drive out talent.

section_notes.keyIdea: Corporate culture — the shared values, beliefs, and norms within an organisation — is invisible but powerful, shaping how decisions are made, how employees behave, and how customers perceive the brand.
takeaway: Culture = shared values and norms; invisible but shapes all decisions.
Strong culture: consistency and motivation, but potential resistance to change.
Culture clash is the top reason mergers fail.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to evaluate whether a firm's culture supports or hinders its strategy. Link culture to specific decisions: would a risk-averse culture support diversification? Would a hierarchical culture support innovation?
section_notes.misconception: Students say strong culture is always good. Wrong because a strong culture that resists change can be fatal in disrupted markets. Instead write: strong culture is an advantage when it supports the firm's strategy, but becomes a liability when the environment changes and the culture prevents adaptation.

steps: Identify stakeholders affected by the decision
Assess power and interest (Mendelow)
Manage conflicts between competing interests
flow.result: Successful firms balance stakeholder needs rather than ignoring any group

section_notes.title: Stakeholder Influences

items.text: Stakeholder — any individual or group with an interest in the activities and decisions of a business: shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, the community, government.
Mendelow's power-interest matrix classifies stakeholders by their power to influence decisions and their level of interest, helping managers prioritise engagement.
Shareholder vs stakeholder debate: should the firm maximise shareholder value (Friedman) or balance the interests of all stakeholders (Freeman)?
Shareholders want maximum dividends; employees want higher wages — paying more in wages reduces profit available for dividends.
Customers want low prices; shareholders want high margins — meeting both requires efficiency gains.
Examiners expect you to identify the stakeholder conflict in a case study and evaluate whose interests should take priority, using Mendelow's matrix or the shareholder/stakeholder models.

section_notes.keyIdea: Business decisions affect multiple stakeholder groups whose interests often conflict — managing these tensions is a key leadership skill and a common exam evaluation theme.
takeaway: Stakeholders have different and often conflicting interests.
Mendelow's matrix: prioritise high power + high interest stakeholders.
The shareholder vs stakeholder debate is central to business ethics questions.
section_notes.examMatters: Every 20-mark Business question involves stakeholder analysis. Identify who gains, who loses, and evaluate the trade-offs. Use Mendelow's matrix to justify which stakeholders should have the most influence.
section_notes.misconception: Students say firms should satisfy all stakeholders equally. Wrong because stakeholders have different levels of power and interest — trying to please everyone equally leads to strategic paralysis. Instead write: use Mendelow's matrix to prioritise stakeholders with high power and high interest, while monitoring others.

steps: Firm faces ethical dilemma
Choose profit maximisation or ethical approach
Ethical approach may cost short-term but build long-term brand value
flow.result: Ethical business can be both morally right and commercially smart — but not always

section_notes.title: Business Ethics and CSR

items.text: Business ethics — the moral principles that guide business behaviour and decision-making, often going beyond what is legally required.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) — the voluntary commitment by a business to act ethically and contribute to economic development while improving the quality of life of employees, the community, and society.
For ethics/CSR: enhanced brand reputation, customer loyalty, employee motivation, reduced regulatory risk, long-term profitability.
Against: Friedman argues the only responsibility of business is to make profit for shareholders; CSR spending diverts resources from core business and may be 'greenwashing'.
The key evaluation: is CSR genuine or strategic? If it genuinely improves stakeholder welfare AND enhances brand value, it creates a win-win. If it is superficial marketing, it can backfire.
Ethics links to stakeholder management: a firm that ignores ethical considerations risks reputational damage, boycotts, and regulatory intervention.

section_notes.keyIdea: Ethics and corporate social responsibility go beyond legal compliance — they represent voluntary choices about how a firm treats its stakeholders, the environment, and society, and they increasingly affect brand value and customer loyalty.
takeaway: Ethics = voluntary standards above legal minimum; CSR = responsible business practices.
Friedman: profit is the only responsibility. Freeman: balance all stakeholder interests.
Evaluate whether CSR is genuine or 'greenwashing'.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners expect balanced evaluation. Don't just say 'CSR is good' — consider the cost, whether it is genuine, and whether it actually improves stakeholder welfare. Use Friedman vs Freeman as your theoretical framework.
section_notes.misconception: Students say CSR always increases profit. Wrong because some CSR initiatives are costly and may not generate a measurable return. Instead write: CSR can enhance brand value and customer loyalty, but the relationship between ethical behaviour and profitability is not automatic — it depends on execution, authenticity, and market context.

section_quiz.question: Which of Handy's cultural types is MOST suited to a large, bureaucratic organisation?
section_quiz.explanation: Role culture features clear job descriptions, formal procedures, and defined hierarchy — characteristics typical of large bureaucratic organisations.

section_quiz.question: Which cultural type is most commonly found in small entrepreneurial firms?
section_quiz.explanation: Power culture, where control radiates from a central figure with few formal rules, is most common in small entrepreneurial firms with a dominant founder.

section_quiz.question: A strong corporate culture can be a DISADVANTAGE because it may lead to:
section_quiz.explanation: While strong cultures have many benefits, they can lead to groupthink — where employees are reluctant to challenge established thinking — and resistance to necessary change.

options: Milton Friedman's view that profit is the primary business purpose
section_quiz.question: The shareholder model of business is most closely associated with:
section_quiz.explanation: Milton Friedman advocated shareholder primacy — arguing that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits within the rules of the game.

section_quiz.question: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL stakeholder?
section_quiz.explanation: The local community is an external stakeholder — it is affected by the business's activities but is not directly part of the organisation. Managers, shareholders, and employees are internal.

options: Misleading claims about a company's environmental practices
section_quiz.question: Greenwashing refers to:
section_quiz.explanation: Greenwashing is when a company makes superficial or misleading claims about its environmental responsibility to appear more ethical than it actually is.

options: Paying fair wages may increase labour costs
Increasing advertising spend to boost sales
section_quiz.question: Which of the following is a TRADE-OFF between ethics and profit?
section_quiz.explanation: Paying fair wages is an ethical choice that increases costs, potentially reducing short-term profits — a classic ethics vs profit trade-off.

options: It happens immediately with new leadership
section_quiz.question: How long do experts estimate genuine cultural change takes?
section_quiz.explanation: Cultural change involves shifting deeply held attitudes and behaviours, which experts suggest takes 3-5 years or more to genuinely embed.

options: It reduces costs by ignoring wider responsibilities
It builds long-term value through strong relationships and reputation
It simplifies decision-making by focusing only on shareholders
section_quiz.question: A key argument FOR the stakeholder model is that:
section_quiz.explanation: The stakeholder model argues that considering all stakeholders builds long-term value through stronger relationships, better reputation, and greater sustainability.

section_practice.guidance: Corporate culture refers to the shared values, beliefs, attitudes and norms that characterise how people behave within an organisation (1 mark). It shapes the way decisions are made — for example, a risk-averse culture may lead to conservative decisions that avoid innovation (1 mark), while an entrepreneurial culture may encourage bold investments and experimentation (1 mark). Culture develops over time and is influenced by leadership, company history, and the industry environment (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Define the term 'corporate culture' and explain how it can influence decision-making. (4 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Profit maximisation argument: shareholders invested in R&D expecting returns, and high pricing funds future research (1 mark); patent protection gives the company legal pricing power (1 mark).

Ethical argument: life-saving medication creates a moral obligation to ensure access, especially for vulnerable populations (1 mark); exploitative pricing risks reputational damage, government intervention, or forced generic competition (1 mark).

Possible resolution: tiered pricing — charging higher prices in wealthy countries while offering lower prices in developing countries — could balance both objectives (1 mark). Long-term brand value and social licence to operate may actually be enhanced by ethical pricing, benefiting shareholders indirectly (1 mark).
section_practice.question: PharmaLife has developed a life-saving medication costing £500 million in R&D. It could price the drug at £50,000 per treatment to maximise returns, or £15,000 to make it accessible in developing countries. Analyse the potential conflict between ethical objectives and profit maximisation. (6 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Argument that short-termism is damaging: reduced R&D weakens the product pipeline and future competitiveness (2 marks); cutting training reduces employee skills and productivity, and may cause quality problems (2 marks); prioritising short-term profits over investment creates a cycle of decline, and talented employees may leave (1 mark).

Counter-argument: meeting profit targets maintains investor confidence and share price in the short term (2 marks); in rapidly changing industries, long-term planning may be unreliable anyway (1 mark).

Judgement: for a manufacturing business, which typically requires sustained investment in technology and skills, three years of cuts suggests a structural problem rather than a temporary adjustment. The short-term gains are likely to be outweighed by long-term competitive decline (2 marks).
section_practice.question: A publicly listed manufacturing company has cut its R&D budget and employee training programmes for three consecutive years to meet quarterly profit targets. Assess the extent to which short-termism damages long-term business performance. (10 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Introduction: Define stakeholders and distinguish between shareholder primacy and stakeholder theory (2 marks).

For moral obligation: businesses depend on stakeholders for their success — exploitative practices cause real harm to vulnerable workers (3 marks); growing consumer awareness means unethical practices are increasingly punished through boycotts and social media campaigns (2 marks); Carroll's CSR pyramid suggests ethical and philanthropic responsibilities exist beyond legal and economic ones (2 marks); long-term sustainability requires healthy communities and environments (2 marks).

Against: Friedman argued the only social responsibility of business is to increase profits within the law (2 marks); shareholders bear financial risk and deserve priority; ethical obligations beyond the law are subjective and vary across cultures (2 marks); competitive markets may not allow ethical premiums — consumers demand low prices which drive the business model (2 marks).

Evaluation: The shareholder-stakeholder divide is often a false dichotomy — satisfied stakeholders frequently contribute to long-term shareholder value through loyalty, productivity and brand strength. For the fast-fashion retailer, the growing trend towards ethical consumerism means that ignoring worker welfare increasingly threatens the business itself, not just its reputation. The most successful modern businesses find ways to align stakeholder and shareholder interests rather than treating them as competing priorities (3 marks).
section_practice.question: A large fast-fashion retailer has been criticised for using suppliers in developing countries that pay low wages and have poor working conditions, while shareholders have benefited from strong profit growth. Evaluate the view that businesses have a moral obligation to consider the interests of all stakeholders, not just shareholders. (20 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Shareholder approach: decisions are primarily aimed at maximising financial returns for shareholders through profit maximisation and dividend growth (1 mark); associated with Friedman's view that the social responsibility of business is to increase profits (1 mark).

Stakeholder approach: decisions consider the interests of all groups affected by the business, including employees, customers, suppliers, communities and the environment (1 mark); associated with Freeman's stakeholder theory, which may involve accepting lower short-term profits for broader long-term benefits (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Outline the difference between a shareholder approach and a stakeholder approach to business decision-making. (4 marks)

steps: An innovative, adaptable culture (task culture) encourages employees to embrace change and take initiative.
When new strategies are introduced, employees adapt willingly — reducing resistance and accelerating implementation.
Faster implementation gives the firm a competitive advantage over rivals with rigid, bureaucratic cultures.
However, a deeply embedded culture can become a constraint if it resists necessary change — making transformation difficult.
chains.title: Corporate culture shapes how strategy is implemented
chains.result: Culture is a strategic asset when aligned with objectives — but a liability when it prevents adaptation to new competitive realities.

steps: A business adopts ethical sourcing and fair trade practices despite higher input costs.
The ethical stance is communicated through marketing, building a reputation for social responsibility.
Ethically-minded consumers develop stronger loyalty and willingness to pay a premium.
Over time, premium pricing and loyalty offset higher costs — while positive PR attracts new customers and quality employees.
chains.title: Ethical decisions build long-term brand value
chains.result: Ethical decision-making can create sustainable competitive advantage through enhanced brand value — but only if commitment is genuine and visible.

steps: Automation and AI reduce labour costs, minimise errors and increase production speed and consistency.
Big data analytics enables precise customer segmentation, personalised marketing and evidence-based decision-making.
E-commerce and digital channels reduce distribution costs and expand market reach beyond geographic boundaries.
However, digital transformation requires significant investment in technology, skills and cybersecurity.
chains.title: Technology transforms operations and marketing
chains.result: Technology is a major driver of efficiency and market reach — but firms that fail to invest risk being disrupted by digitally-native competitors.

steps: A business integrates CSR into its core strategy — investing in community programmes, carbon reduction and supply chain transparency.
Stronger stakeholder relationships reduce the risk of regulatory penalties, consumer boycotts and reputational damage.
Investors increasingly prioritise ESG criteria, viewing CSR-committed firms as lower risk with better long-term prospects.
However, CSR must be genuine — superficial 'greenwashing' is quickly exposed and damages credibility more than doing nothing.
chains.title: CSR strengthens stakeholder relationships and reduces risk
chains.result: Strategic CSR enhances long-term business value by building stakeholder trust — but it requires authentic commitment, not just marketing.

evaluation.title: Ethical behaviour is not always profitable
evaluation.content: In price-competitive markets, consumers may prioritise low prices over ethics. The commercial return on ethical investment depends on the target market, visibility of practices and whether competitors also adopt similar standards. Premium and niche markets benefit more.

evaluation.title: Data-driven decisions have limits
evaluation.content: Big data provides powerful insights but is only as good as the data itself — biased or outdated data leads to flawed conclusions. Over-reliance on quantitative data risks neglecting creativity, intuition and ethical judgement. GDPR also constrains data collection.

evaluation.title: Culture change is notoriously difficult
evaluation.content: Changing an embedded culture requires sustained effort, leadership change and time. Quick fixes rarely work. A culture that was once a strength can become a weakness if the competitive environment shifts. The most resilient firms build cultures that value adaptability itself.

section_common_mistakes.title: Treating All Stakeholder Interests as Equal
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Acknowledge that stakeholder conflicts require trade-offs. Examiners reward candidates who show awareness that balancing interests is complex, not straightforward.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming all stakeholders have equal power and influence over business decisions.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Stakeholders have different levels of power and interest. Use stakeholder mapping to identify which groups are most influential. In practice, firms must prioritise — they cannot satisfy all stakeholders equally.

section_common_mistakes.title: Confusing Strong Culture with Good Culture
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Always evaluate whether the CONTENT of the culture is beneficial, not just its strength. A strong culture of complacency is worse than a weak culture open to new ideas.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a strong culture is always positive for the organisation.
section_common_mistakes.correction: A strong culture means values are widely shared — but those values could be negative (e.g. resistance to change, exclusionary). Strong cultures can also lead to groupthink and make adaptation difficult.

section_common_mistakes.title: Describing CSR as Purely Altruistic
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Examiners value nuanced analysis — is the firm's CSR genuine commitment or strategic marketing? The concept of 'greenwashing' is a useful evaluative tool.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Presenting CSR as purely charitable behaviour with no business benefit.
section_common_mistakes.correction: CSR often serves strategic purposes — enhancing reputation, attracting customers and investors, retaining talent, and reducing regulatory risk. The best answers explore whether CSR is genuinely motivated or primarily a business strategy.

section_common_mistakes.title: Listing Handy's Culture Types Without Application
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Application marks require you to link theory to context. Don't describe all four types — focus on the most relevant one and analyse its impact.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Describing all four of Handy's culture types without linking them to the specific business in the case study.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Identify which culture type BEST describes the firm in the scenario and explain WHY. Then evaluate whether this culture helps or hinders the firm's strategy.

section_common_mistakes.title: Oversimplifying the Ethics vs Profit Trade-Off
section_common_mistakes.examTip: The best evaluation considers both short-term and long-term perspectives. Ethical behaviour may cost more now but create sustainable competitive advantage over time.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Presenting ethics and profit as always in direct conflict — implying firms must choose one or the other.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Ethical behaviour can ENHANCE long-term profitability through reputation, loyalty, and risk reduction. The trade-off is more nuanced — short-term costs of ethical behaviour may lead to long-term financial gains.
